_comment: WheatGuard AI – Disease Information Database. Each key matches a class name discovered from the dataset. All recommendations are general guidance only. Consult a local agricultural extension officer for confirmed treatment.

Healthy.description: The wheat plant shows no visible signs of disease or stress. Leaves are green and uniform.
symptoms: Uniform green colouration
No lesions, pustules, or discolouration
Normal leaf and stem structure
prevention: Continue current agronomic practices
Monitor regularly for early signs of stress or disease
Maintain balanced soil nutrition
Ensure adequate drainage to prevent waterlogging
management: No immediate intervention required
Continue scheduled scouting every 7–10 days
Record field observations for future reference
Healthy.disclaimer: AI prediction indicates a healthy plant. Regular scouting remains important as early-stage infections may not yet be visually apparent.

Leaf_Rust.description: Leaf rust is caused by the fungal pathogen Puccinia triticina. It is one of the most widespread wheat diseases worldwide, capable of causing significant yield losses when conditions favour rapid spread.
symptoms: Small, round to oval orange-brown pustules (uredinia) on the upper leaf surface
Pustules scattered irregularly across the leaf blade
Yellowing around pustule clusters in severe infections
Black telia (teliospores) may appear late in the season
Leaves may turn yellow and dry prematurely
favourable_conditions: Dense canopy with poor air circulation
prevention: Plant resistant or tolerant wheat varieties
Use certified, disease-free seed
Rotate crops to break disease cycles
Avoid late planting that extends the green crop period
Remove or plough in crop residues after harvest
Apply balanced fertilisation — avoid excessive nitrogen
management: Scout fields regularly and monitor pustule development
Apply foliar fungicides at first sign of infection (consult local extension for registered products)
A second application may be needed if infection pressure remains high
Do not delay treatment — early intervention prevents exponential spread
Leaf_Rust.disclaimer: This is an AI-based prediction and NOT a confirmed diagnosis. Yield loss can reach 20–40% in susceptible varieties under high infection pressure. Consult a certified agronomist or agricultural extension officer before applying any chemical treatment.

Yellow_Rust.description: Yellow rust, also called stripe rust, is caused by Puccinia striiformis f. sp. tritici. It spreads rapidly under cool, moist conditions and can cause severe yield losses if untreated.
symptoms: Pale yellow to bright yellow pustules arranged in characteristic stripes along the leaf veins
Stripes run parallel to the leaf midrib
Leaves may turn entirely yellow-brown in severe cases
White to grey fungal spore masses visible under humid conditions
Infection can spread to leaf sheaths, glumes, and awns
favourable_conditions: Cloudy, humid weather prolonging spore viability
High-density plantings with poor air circulation
prevention: Select certified rust-resistant varieties
Use treated, disease-free seed
Sow at recommended times to avoid peak cool-humid periods
Manage crop density through appropriate seeding rates
Remove and destroy infected crop debris
Avoid excess nitrogen fertilisation
management: Apply registered foliar fungicides (triazoles or strobilurins) at flag-leaf or early infection stage
Repeat application as per label instructions if disease pressure persists
Prioritise treatment of high-value or susceptible fields
Report new virulent races to local plant protection authorities
Yellow_Rust.disclaimer: AI prediction only. Yellow rust can cause yield losses exceeding 70% under epidemic conditions. Seek confirmation from an agricultural extension officer before applying fungicides.

Stem_Rust.description: Stem rust is caused by Puccinia graminis f. sp. tritici. Once a devastating global threat, new virulent races such as Ug99 have re-emerged as serious concerns for wheat production.
symptoms: Large, brick-red to dark brown elongated pustules on stems and leaf sheaths
Pustules tear through the epidermis, giving a rough, ragged appearance
Spilled spore masses stain fingers rust-red/brown
Severely infected stems weaken and lodge (fall over)
Black teliospores appear late season, giving the 'black rust' appearance
prevention: Use resistant varieties (critical first line of defence)
Eradicate common barberry (alternate host) near fields
Plant early to avoid peak spore periods
Monitor for emergence of new races through national surveillance programs
management: Foliar fungicide application at early stem rust onset can reduce damage
Prioritise treatment of susceptible fields
Report unusual or severe stem rust outbreaks to local authorities immediately
Consult local extension services for registered fungicide options
Stem_Rust.disclaimer: Stem rust is a serious yield-threatening disease. This is an AI prediction, not a diagnosis. Contact your national wheat disease surveillance programme and a certified agronomist immediately if stem rust is suspected.

Powdery_Mildew.description: Powdery mildew is caused by the obligate biotrophic fungus Blumeria graminis f. sp. tritici. It thrives in dense canopies with moderate temperatures and high humidity.
symptoms: White to greyish powdery fungal colonies on upper leaf surfaces
Fluffy, superficial mycelium easily wiped off at first but becomes denser
Yellowing of leaf tissue beneath fungal colonies
Affected leaves may senesce prematurely
Small, dark cleistothecia (fruiting bodies) visible in late season
favourable_conditions: High humidity without free moisture (unlike rusts)
Excessive nitrogen fertilisation promoting lush growth
prevention: Choose mildew-resistant varieties
Avoid excessive nitrogen application
Optimise plant density to improve air circulation
Use balanced fertilisation (phosphorus and potassium strengthen resistance)
management: Apply foliar fungicides at early disease onset
Triazole-based fungicides are generally effective
Avoid applications during heavy rain or when crop is moisture-stressed
Follow resistance management guidelines by rotating fungicide classes
Powdery_Mildew.disclaimer: AI prediction only. Powdery mildew severity varies widely by variety and environment. Consult an agricultural extension officer before applying fungicide treatments.

Septoria_Leaf_Blotch.description: Septoria tritici blotch is caused by the fungus Zymoseptoria tritici (formerly Mycosphaerella graminicola). It is one of the most economically important foliar diseases of wheat in temperate regions.
symptoms: Irregular pale to tan-green lesions on leaves
Lesions bounded by leaf veins, giving a blocky appearance
Small black dots (pycnidia) visible within lesions — a key diagnostic feature
Lesions expand and coalesce, covering large leaf areas
Lower leaves affected first; infection progresses upwards
favourable_conditions: Rain splash spreading spores between plants
prevention: Use certified STB-resistant varieties
Treat seed with fungicide to reduce primary inoculum
Plough crop residues to reduce spore load
Avoid dense seeding rates
Apply nitrogen responsibly
management: Apply fungicides at GS31–32 (stem extension) and again at flag-leaf if needed
Triazole or SDHI-based fungicides show good efficacy
Timely application is critical — STB is difficult to control once widespread
Rotate fungicide chemistry to delay resistance development
Septoria_Leaf_Blotch.disclaimer: AI prediction only. STB is a major yield-reducing disease in humid climates. Confirm diagnosis with an agronomist and consult local extension recommendations before applying treatments.

Fusarium_Head_Blight.description: Fusarium head blight (FHB) is caused primarily by Fusarium graminearum. Beyond yield loss, it contaminates grain with mycotoxins (deoxynivalenol / DON) that are harmful to humans and livestock.
Fusarium_Head_Blight.causal_agent: Fusarium graminearum and related Fusarium spp. (fungi)
symptoms: Premature bleaching of individual spikelets or partial heads
Pink to salmon-orange fungal sporulation at the base of bleached spikelets
Shrivelled, lightweight grain (Fusarium-damaged kernels)
Brown discolouration of glumes at the infection point
Entire heads may blight in severe infections
favourable_conditions: Warm, wet weather during anthesis (flowering) — critical infection window
Continuous cereal cropping increasing inoculum levels
Maize or wheat stubble on field surface
prevention: Plant FHB-resistant or tolerant varieties
Rotate crops to break disease cycles (avoid continuous wheat or wheat after maize)
Plough in infected crop residues
Avoid planting in low-lying, poorly drained fields
Optimise timing of nitrogen to avoid excessive canopy
management: Apply registered fungicides at early flowering (GS60–65) for best efficacy
Triazole fungicides (e.g., tebuconazole) have best label efficacy
Do not consume or feed suspected mycotoxin-contaminated grain to livestock without testing
Report confirmed outbreaks to grain buyers and local health authorities
Fusarium_Head_Blight.disclaimer: IMPORTANT: Fusarium head blight can produce mycotoxins hazardous to human and animal health. This is an AI prediction, NOT a confirmed diagnosis or food-safety clearance. Contact an agricultural extension officer and arrange grain mycotoxin testing before use.

Tan_Spot.description: Tan spot is caused by the necrotrophic fungus Pyrenophora tritici-repentis. It is favoured by conservation tillage practices that leave infected residue on the soil surface.
symptoms: Tan to brown oval or diamond-shaped lesions with a yellow halo
A distinctive dark-brown centre with a yellow chlorotic zone is characteristic
Lesions may coalesce causing large necrotic areas
Lower canopy affected first, progressing upward
favourable_conditions: Wet or humid conditions following dry periods
Infected wheat residue on or near the soil surface
prevention: Rotate crops (break the residue inoculum cycle)
Incorporate residues by tillage where practical
Use resistant varieties
Avoid excessive nitrogen that promotes dense canopy
management: Apply foliar fungicides at early tillering if disease pressure is high
Triazole and strobilurin fungicides provide useful control
Prioritise residue management for long-term control
Tan_Spot.disclaimer: AI prediction only. Consult an agricultural extension officer to confirm diagnosis and recommend appropriate management strategies for local conditions.

Ensure the image is in focus and shows representative symptoms
management: Consult a local agricultural extension officer or certified plant pathologist
Collect a physical sample for laboratory diagnosis if symptoms persist
